name: Glen Canyon National Recreation Area
author: author-D-2026-10-18
summary:
Behind the Bureau of Reclamation’s Glen Canyon Dam, the Colorado River and its tributaries back up about 185 miles to form Lake Powell, set among buttes, mesas and cliffs where Navajo sandstone is the dominant rock. Work on the concrete arch dam began in 1956; its last two generating units came on line in 1966, and the lake reached full pool in 1980, 1983 and 1984. The brochure calls the dam a project born amid controversy and compromise. [1] A 2000 historic structures report’s chronology dates the recreation area’s establishment, by agreement between the Bureau of Reclamation and the Park Service, to April 18, 1958; [1] the 2014 Foundation Document dates its establishment by Congress to October 27, 1972. It covers more than 1.25 million acres of northern Arizona and southeastern Utah, its southern boundary runs beside the Navajo Nation for almost 500 miles, and it borders Rainbow Bridge National Monument, proclaimed in 1910. [1]

Its Foundation Document says the area preserves a record of more than 10,000 years of human presence. About 2,500 cultural sites have been recorded, though only 3 percent of the land has been surveyed, and some boaters damage shoreline sites through unauthorized excavation, artifact collecting and pervasive graffiti. [1] Some of that history now lies under water: the Crossing of the Fathers, where the Spanish priests Domínguez and Escalante cut steps into the sandstone at Padre Creek on November 7, 1776, is beneath Padre Bay, and the ferry town of Hite was flooded by the lake. John Wesley Powell, who named Glen Canyon on his 1869 voyage, is the lake’s namesake. [1]

indigenous.html:
Park staff consult regularly with the Hopi Tribe, Kaibab Paiute Tribe, Navajo Nation, Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah, Pueblo of Zuni, San Juan Southern Paiute and Ute Mountain Ute. For many indigenous peoples of the Four Corners region, Rainbow Bridge is, in the Foundation Document’s words, a spiritually occupied landscape inseparable from their cultural identities. [1] In 2011 research, Hopi cultural advisors identified 33 cultural resources with traditional Hopi associations; Hopi people use Itaakuku, “our footprints,” for places where the ancestors lived. Rainbow Bridge, Namiqw’wunu to the Hopi, is tied to six clans. A Hopi shrine there was submerged during high water in Lake Powell; clan members still visit to leave prayer feathers. [1]

Southern Paiute traditional lands, a 1994 study reports, are bounded by more than 600 miles of Piapaxa, the Colorado River, which, by traditional belief, the Creator charged Paiute people to protect and manage; one San Juan Southern Paiute elder likened the river to the veins of the world. [1]

climate.html: The park’s resources and visitor experiences depend on water, the 2014 Foundation Document says, and its lake levels fluctuate widely; projections, it adds, indicate there may be longer or more frequent droughts. Writing in 2014, it cited climate-change models projecting higher temperatures, no increase in precipitation, reduced runoff and reduced storage in Lake Powell by 2021. Fluctuating levels force frequent moves of marina infrastructure, and at very low levels launch ramps may become unusable; at lower reservoir levels lake water does not reach beneath Rainbow Bridge. As drought persists, the document notes, parties with water rights are seeking to install pipelines to draw water from the lake. [1]
